questions.prompt: State CampusOps' stock invariant and explain how Part and the in-memory store protect it, including the overflow guard and the snapshot discipline.

keyPoints.text: Consuming reserved stock lowers both OnHand and Reserved, so Available is unchanged.
keyPoints.quote: consumption decreases both physical stock and its reserved portion

keyPoints.text: Releasing must go through the release command, not a negative reservation.
keyPoints.quote: A negative reservation is not a clever way to release stock

keyPoints.text: The capacity check is written as a subtraction that cannot overflow.
keyPoints.quote: which is safe because existing stock is nonnegative

keyPoints.text: The guard must run before any state changes.
keyPoints.quote: Throwing after assignment would be too late

keyPoints.text: Callers never get a live reference to stored parts.
keyPoints.quote: The repaired adapter copies on insertion and on reads

keyPoints.text: MemberwiseClone is shallow, so a future mutable field would be shared.
keyPoints.quote: a shallow clone would share that list

keyPoints.text: Safety comes from reasoning about ownership, not from a rule of thumb.
keyPoints.quote: explain the ownership of every referenced object

questions.prompt: Why did two thread-safe containers not make reservations safe, what does the single lock guarantee, and how does that translate to EF Core?

keyPoints.text: Per-call safety does not compose into a business transaction.
keyPoints.quote: A dictionary and queue can each be safe for concurrent calls while the combined business operation remains unsafe

keyPoints.text: The repair covers stock and history with one lock.
keyPoints.quote: One private lock protects both inventory and reservation history

keyPoints.text: Readers take the same lock, so half-committed states are invisible.
keyPoints.quote: They cannot observe an ordinary intermediate state with only one side committed

keyPoints.text: The guarantee stops at the process boundary.
keyPoints.quote: This is a single-process memory guarantee

keyPoints.text: A database version needs a real transaction across both tables.
keyPoints.quote: A database implementation needs one real transaction over both tables

keyPoints.text: Read-then-check-then-update in two statements oversells.
keyPoints.quote: Two connections both pass the check

keyPoints.text: Rollback does not undo in-memory entity changes.
keyPoints.quote: a rolled-back transaction restores the database, not your C# objects

questions.prompt: Explain CampusOps' cancellation boundary, why atomic reservations are still not retry-safe, and what the authentication, authorization and existence checks do and do not prove.

keyPoints.text: Cancellation is honoured only before the commit.
keyPoints.quote: Before a reservation commit, the store checks it and changes nothing

keyPoints.text: After a commit, reporting cancellation would mislead the client.
keyPoints.quote: Reporting cancellation after committing could encourage the client to retry an operation that already happened

keyPoints.text: Without an idempotency key, a repeated request is a new reservation.
keyPoints.quote: repeating the same request can reserve more stock

keyPoints.text: Atomicity and retries are separate concerns.
keyPoints.quote: Atomicity and retry safety are different promises

keyPoints.text: Missing identity and insufficient role produce different statuses.
keyPoints.quote: Missing demo identity receives 401; a Technician receives 403

keyPoints.text: The work-order existence check is not an ownership or status check.
keyPoints.quote: It does not prove campus ownership or enforce all order statuses
